rationale: The book's core identification of pearl as the full moon (one complete light governing appointed times and serving as the merchant's entry-gate) requires numerous unsupported retranslations, poem-as-sky-portrait allegories, letter-plays, and phase-symbolism steps that create internal contradictions with its own cited texts. The standard kingdom-as-supreme-treasure reading of the unkeyed parable accounts for the same NT contexts, parallel treasure parable, value comparisons, and Rev 21 gates with far fewer leaps and no self-contradiction, while still allowing secondary preciousness or luxury senses elsewhere.
book_core_identification: Pearl is the one complete light—the full moon (keseh/fulness)—governor of the appointed times (moedim), whose one-pearl gates are the merchant's entry at the King's gate.
book_secondary_elaborations: peninim recovered from KJV 'rubies' as the parable's pearls
Proverbs 3 and 31 poems re-rendered line-by-line as bare-letter portraits of the moon/bride (rising at night, lamp not out, palms holding the circuit, etc.)
keseh shares letters/root with throne (kisse') and means full moon rather than merely 'time appointed'
east-gate opening on new-moon day admits the full moon as true entrance; dark-moon is the counterfeit climber
Matt 7:6 pearls-before-swine = holy times trampled by nations
paired treasure/pearl parables welded via Isa 33:6 (times + treasure)
calendar implications for month-start and sabbaths deferred to another book
strongest_counter_interpretation: The pearl primarily symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven (or the salvation/gospel/Christ found in it) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing worth that one should gladly surrender everything else to obtain; by extension it stands for sacred precious spiritual truth (with a secondary negative sense as worldly luxury in other contexts).
counter_core_identification: Pearl = Kingdom of Heaven / supreme spiritual treasure of incomparable value (Matt 13:45-46 primary; Matt 7:6 and Rev 21:21 supporting).
material_core_denial: The pearl is not the full moon, the governor of appointed times, or the merchant's entry-gate; those are not its referent in the parable or the supporting texts.
counter_case: Matthew 13:44-46 presents the pearl parable back-to-back with the treasure-in-field parable; both illustrate the identical point that the kingdom is worth selling all to obtain, so the pearl (like the treasure) is the kingdom itself of supreme value, not a later-derived gate or moon phase.

The grammar and context of the kingdom parables require no OT moon derivation or re-pointing; Jesus' own audience and the Teacher's later explanations of other parables confirm the value-of-the-kingdom sense without residual symbols left for modern concordance work.

Proverbs 3:15 and 31:10 simply use peninim (whether pearls or rubies) as a conventional high-value comparison item; wisdom and the virtuous woman are 'more precious than' costly jewels—exactly parallel to other biblical value sayings—without any need to identify the jewels themselves as the moon or the woman.

Matthew 7:6 and Revelation 21:21 continue the same preciousness/glory sense (holy things not to be profaned; city of the kingdom adorned with single-pearl gates) without forcing a full-moon or moedim calendar reading.
Negative pearl uses (1 Tim 2:9; Rev 17–18) as ostentatious luxury fit the same ordinary precious-object range and require no special lunar exception.

The book's method itself (derive every unkeyed parable solely from prior OT patterns) is applied inconsistently: the parallel treasure parable is left as kingdom-value while the pearl is forced into a different gate/moon slot, and many 'attestations' are single-verse or post-hoc letter plays rather than multi-witness established symbols.
book_explanatory_advantages: Attempts to give a single consistent referent for 'one pearl' across the parable, Rev 21:21 gates, and the completeness/roundness of the full moon
Links the unkeyed parable to OT merchant/merchandise vocabulary and the peninim recovery
Offers a unified reading of the moon as bride/faithful witness already developed in the book's prior light chapters
counter_explanatory_advantages: Directly accounts for the kingdom-parable frame and the identical 'sell all to obtain' logic of the adjacent treasure parable with zero retranslation or sky-allegory steps
Preserves the ordinary value-comparison sense of Prov 3:15/31:10 without generating a self-comparison contradiction
Fits Matt 7:6 (pearls = holy/precious things) and Rev 21:21 (pearl gates = kingdom glory) as natural extensions of the same preciousness motif
Requires no acceptance of unpointed letter-plays, poem-as-moon-portrait claims, or calendar overhauls; fewer and smaller unsupported inferences overall
Matches the broad, multi-tradition consensus on the dominant positive symbolism while still accommodating secondary luxury senses
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Proverbs 31:10 (and 3:15): the virtuous woman/wisdom is priced 'far above pearls/peninim,' yet the book identifies both that woman/bride and the pearl itself as the full moon, producing a direct contradiction (the moon is far above the moon).

Matthew 13:44-46 structure: the pearl parable is presented as the exact twin of the treasure-in-field parable, both teaching the supreme value of the kingdom by the act of selling all; a full-moon/gate reading severs that parallel and leaves the kingdom-likeness of the merchant seeking moons unexplained without further non-textual invention.
decisive_sources: Psalm 104:19; Genesis 1:14 (moon for seasons—used by book but not requiring pearl = moon)
unresolved_objections: The recovery of peninim as 'pearl' (Strong's) and the 'one' emphasis in Rev 21:21 remain interesting lexical observations even if they do not compel the full-moon identification
The book's larger symbolic-language method and prior light chapters are not re-litigated here; only their application to this term fails the comparative test
